# Introduction 
Individuals with hearing disabilities in Indonesia face significant communication barriers due to limited public proficiency in Indonesian Sign Language (BISINDO), creating an urgent need for real-time translation tools [1], [2]. Previous studies have explored machine learning for gesture classification [3], [4], [5], [6], with Swasono et al. successfully utilizing YOLO11 to recognize six predefined BISINDO phrases in real time [7]. However, this vocabulary size remains limited for practical daily interactions. 

YOLO-based detectors are widely adopted for real-time visual recognition due to their efficiency [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], with YOLOv26 being the most advanced iteration designed for optimal precision and computational speed on edge devices [13]. Yet, expanding a system's vocabulary requires a more complex training set, which risks degrading model accuracy or increasing inference latency. Therefore, this study investigates the effect of training set expansion from an established baseline of six phrases to eight phrases—on YOLOv26 performance for real-time BISINDO recognition. By conducting an apple-to-apple comparison under identical experimental settings, this research comprehensively evaluates detection of metrics (such as mAP) alongside real-time indicators (latency and FPS) to determine the model's scalability and stability.
# Literature Review
## Sign Language and Communication
Sign language is a comprehensive visual-manual communication system that employs hand gestures, body postures, and facial expressions to construct and convey linguistic meaning. Within the Indonesian context, two major linguistic frameworks exist: Bahasa Isyarat Indonesia (BISINDO), which developed naturally as the native language of the Indonesian Deaf community, and Sistem Isyarat Bahasa Indonesia (SIBI), a structured sign system primarily designed for formal educational settings. A persistent lack of general public awareness regarding sign language continues to enforce communication barriers between the Deaf and hearing communities [14]. To bridge this systemic gap, recent research focuses heavily on expanding the dataset boundaries for complex dialects and regional hand structures [15], [16], [17] 
## Real-Time Object Detection (YOLO26)
The You Only Look Once (YOLO) family represents the state-of-the-art in single-stage real-time object detection [18]. This research focuses exclusively on YOLO26, a highly streamlined iteration engineered explicitly for edge-device efficiency and deployment-ready performance without architectural bloat [13].

Native End-to-End Predictor: Unlike traditional architectures that rely on computationally expensive post-processing, YOLO26 eliminates Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) via a native end-to-end framework, effectively resolving the latency bottlenecks common in mobile and edge pipelines [13].

Streamlined Regression Head: By completely removing Distribution Focal Loss (DFL), YOLO26 simplifies the regression loss computation, allowing the model to achieve up to a 43% faster CPU inference speed while maintaining equivalent or superior accuracy-to-latency trade-offs [13].

Small-Object Accuracy: To resolve the challenge of recognizing detailed physical features, YOLO26 introduces Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment (STAL). This training-time refinement mechanism significantly improves the precision of tracking minute finger joint changes and facial landmarks [13].

Scale-Dependent Deployment: Comparative benchmarking confirms that while older iterations excel at extreme nano scales, YOLO26 achieves strict statistical superiority at large and extra-large scales with substantial advantages in mean Average Precision, making it optimal for complex structural tasks like gesture isolation [19].

## Deep Learning-Based Sign Language Translation and Dataset
Sign Language Translation (SLT) is defined as a complex sequence-to-sequence mapping problem that transforms continuous visual gesture streams into natural language sentences. Recent system overviews show a global shift from simple classification toward comprehensive translation frameworks [17], [18], [20].

Transformer Architectures: The standard implementation for capturing long-term visual-textual dependencies relies heavily on the self-attention mechanism of Transformers. Benchmarking experiments show that standalone Transformers drastically improve linguistic accuracy, delivering a 28.14 point increase in BLEU scores over traditional sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) pipelines [21].

Recurrent Sequential Frameworks: Recurrent units such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) remain common components for isolating temporal gesture patterns [21]. When applied to highly dense sequential gesture datasets, GRU models optimized with Bahdanau attention mechanics have demonstrated exceptional sequence alignment, yielding a ROUGE score of 94.37% [21].

Grammar-Aware Multi-Modality: Modern translation networks prevent errors by treating sign language as a structured language rather than isolated movements. Incorporating multimodal feature fusion (such as 3D body pose keypoints and RGB frames) into a grammar-aware Transformer framework has been shown to outperform traditional unmodal vision models [22].

Autoregressive Sign Production (T2S-GPT): Modern two-stage frameworks utilize Dynamic Vector Quantization (DVQ-VAE) to balance the uneven information density inherent to natural sign language [23]. By dynamically compressing redundant visual frames into compact discrete codes, a specialized generative pre-trained transformer model can autoregressively map spoken text directly to sign code sequences [23]. 

TUD-BISINDO & PHOENIX Datasets: While large-scale international corpora like PHOENIX-News provide up to 486 hours of continuous signing data, the Telkom University Database (TUD)-BISINDO serves as the localized structural training dataset. TUD-BISINDO provides complex multi-angle, variable-lighting environments necessary to ensure that the NMS-free YOLO26 network can maintain its optimal accuracy thresholds under erratic, real-world deployment conditions.
# Methodology
This study uses an experimental comparison strategy to assess how the training set expansion effect YOLO26 recognition performance for real-time BISINDO phrase detection. The same Yolo26 architecture is used to train two models separately under identical configurations: Model A is trained on a six-phrase dataset, and Model B is trained on an eight-phrase dataset that includes all six of Model A's phrases plus two more. Both models are later evaluated on the same six-class test set to provide a direct and fair comparison. As shown in Figure 1, the entire research pipeline consists of five stages: data collecting, data preprocessing, model training, model testing, and comparison result analysis.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. Flowchart
## Data Collection
The dataset in this study covers eight BISINDO phrases: saya, kamu, senang, bingung, marah, apa kabar, terima kasih, and tolong. Model A uses the first six words as its six-class subset from the eight-class, but Model B uses all eight phrases. A unique, dynamic hand gesture made in front of a camera is represented by each sentence.

Data were collected from two sources. For the training and validation sets, gesture data were recorded by the research team using a standard webcam under varied but controlled conditions, including different lighting levels and slight variations in signer position following practices established in recent sign language dataset construction studies [24], [25]. Each gesture was captured as still frames extracted from short video sequences, yielding 300 images per class. For the independent test set, 50 video clips per class were sourced from an existing public BISINDO repository on Kaggle [26] and converted to frames using the same extraction pipeline. The total dataset therefore contains 350 samples per class, with 300 self-recorded samples used for training and validation, and 50 Kaggle-sourced samples reserved exclusively for testing.
## Data Preprocessing
### Frame Extraction
The Kaggle test dataset was originally collected in MP4 video format, published by Pardede [26] and contains 40 BISINDO words with approximately 50 video clips per word. Since YOLO26 operates on static image frames rather than raw video sequences, all test videos were initially converted to individual frames using OpenCV's video capture pipeline. Frames were sampled at a uniform interval to reduce redundancy from consecutive near-identical frames, a commonly adopted practice in sign language video preprocessing [27], [28], [29]. Blurry or transitional frames were eliminated; only those with distinct hand gestures were kept. For each of the eight target phrases, this procedure produced 50 suitable image samples per class, which made up the independent test set. 

For the training and validation data recorded by the research team, each gesture session was also recorded as short video clips and transformed to frames using the same extraction pipeline, producing a total of 300 images per class across all eight phrases.
### Automated Bounding Box Annotation
Rather than relying on manual annotation tools like LabelImg, this study employs MediaPipe's hand landmark detection pipeline to automate bounding box generation for all images [30], [31]. MediaPipe detects 21 keypoints per hand per frame using a two-stage ML pipeline: a palm detector that localizes the hand region in the full image, followed by a hand landmark model that regresses 21 three-dimensional joint coordinates within the detected region [32]. From these 21 landmarks, the minimum enclosing axis-aligned rectangle is computed by taking the minimum and maximum x and y coordinates across all visible keypoints. This rectangle is then expanded by a small padding factor to ensure the full hand region is enclosed, and the resulting coordinates are converted to YOLO annotation format: normalized center x, normalized center y, normalized width, and normalized height relative to the image dimensions.

This automated approach substantially reduces annotation time compared to manual labeling, also reducing inter-annotator inconsistency, consistent with practices reported in recent sign language annotation pipelines [28], [31], [33], [34]. All generated annotations were visually verified on a per-class sample basis and corrected manually where MediaPipe failed to detect the hand, which occurred primarily in images with complex backgrounds or severe lighting variation. Frames for which hand detection consistently failed were excluded from the dataset.
### Dataset Split
The annotated dataset was divided into three non-overlapping subsets. The self-recorded dataset of 300 images per class was split into a training set and a validation set at an 80:20 ratio, insisting on 240 training samples and 60 validation samples per class. The Kaggle-sourced dataset of 50 images per class was reserved exclusively as the independent test set and was not used at any point during training or validation. This design ensures that test set performance reflects genuine generalization to unseen data from an independent source, strengthening the validity of the comparative evaluation.

For Model A (six phrases), the training set contains 1,440 images, the validation set contains 360 images, and the test set contains 300 images. For Model B (eight phrases), the training set contains 1,920 images, the validation set contains 480 images, while the test set remains the same 300 six-class images used for Model A to ensure a direct and fair comparison.

| **Subset** | **Source** | **Per Class** | **Model A (6 phrases)** | **Model B (8 phrases)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Train** | Self-recorded | 240 | 1440 | 1920 |
| **Validation** | Self-recorded | 60 | 360 | 480 |
| **Test** | Kaggle [26]  | 50 | 300 | 300 |
| **Total** |  | 350 | 2100 | 2700 |
### Data Augmentation
To improve model generalization and reduce overfitting given the relatively moderate per-class sample count, data augmentation was applied exclusively to the training set. Augmentation techniques were selected based on established practices for YOLO-based object detection [35]and include horizontal flipping, random rotation within plus or minus 15 degrees, brightness and contrast jittering, Gaussian blur, and random cropping. These photometric and geometric transformations simulate real-world variation in lighting, signer position, and camera angle that a deployed system would encounter.
## Model Training
Both Model A and Model B were built on the YOLO26 architecture, which introduces several key improvements over prior YOLO generations: NMS-free end-to-end inference via one-to-one assignment, the MuSGD optimizer for backbone stabilization, Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment (STAL), and Progressive Loss Balancing (ProgLoss) for dynamic supervision weighting [13]. These properties make YOLO26 particularly suitable for real-time gesture recognition on edge-capable hardware.

Model A was trained exclusively on the six-phrase BISINDO dataset. Model B was trained on the full eight-phrase dataset containing the same six phrases plus two additional classes. Both models used identical training hyperparameters: input resolution 640x640, batch size 16, 100 epochs, and the MuSGD optimizer with a cosine learning rate schedule, following the official YOLO26 training recipe [13]. Transfer learning was applied by initializing both models from the official YOLO26 pretrained weights on COCO prior to fine-tuning on the domain-specific BISINDO dataset, a strategy that has consistently improved convergence speed and generalization in custom object detection tasks.
## Model Testing
Both Model A and Model B were evaluated on the identical six-class test set to ensure that observed performance differences are attributable solely to the difference in training vocabulary. Detection performance was quantified using the following metrics:

Precision measures the proportion of positive detections that are genuinely correct:

*Precision =* 	

Recall measures the proportion of actual positive instances that the model correctly detects:

*Recall =*  	2

F1-Score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, providing a single balanced performance measure:

*F1- Score =*  3

Mean Average Precision (mAP) aggregates per-class detection accuracy across the full class set:

*mAP* *=* 	4

Real-time performance was assessed using Inference latency (ms) and Frames per second (FPS): Computed as 1000 divided by latency. Per-class breakdowns of mAP, precision, and recall were also reported to identify whether specific phrases were disproportionately affected by vocabulary expansion.
## Comparative Result Analysis
Results from Model A and Model B were compared across all evaluation metrics on the shared six-class test set. The analysis examined whether the addition of two new phrases to the training distribution strengthened or weakened recognition of the original six phrases, and whether any patterns emerged at the per-class level that could indicate class interference or generalization improvement. Findings are discussed in the context of prior work on the effect of class count on fine-tuned detection model performance.

# Using the Template
After the text edit has been completed, the paper is ready for the template. Duplicate the template file by using the Save As command, and use the naming convention prescribed by your conference for the name of your paper. In this newly created file, highlight all of the contents and import your prepared text file. You are now ready to style your paper; use the scroll down window on the left of the MS Word Formatting toolbar.
## Authors and Affiliations
**The template is** **designed** **for,** **but not limited to,** **six** **authors.** A minimum of one author is required for all conference articles. Author names should be listed starting from left to right and then moving down to the next line. This is the author sequence that will be used in future citations and by indexing services. Names should not be listed in columns nor group by affiliation. Please keep your affiliations as succinct as possible (for example, do not differentiate among departments of the same organization).
### For papers with more than six authors: Add author names horizontally, moving to a third row if needed for more than 8 authors.
### For papers with less than six authors: To change the default, adjust the template as follows.
#### Selection: Highlight all author and affiliation lines.
#### Change number of columns: Select the Columns icon from the MS Word Standard toolbar and then select the correct number of columns from the selection palette.
#### Deletion: Delete the author and affiliation lines for the extra authors.
## Identify the Headings
Headings, or heads, are organizational devices that guide the reader through your paper. There are two types: component heads and text heads.

Component heads identify the different components of your paper and are not topically subordinate to each other. Examples include Acknowledgments and References and, for these, the correct style to use is “Heading 5”. Use “figure caption” for your Figure captions, and “table head” for your table title. Run-in heads, such as “Abstract”, will require you to apply a style (in this case, italic) in addition to the style provided by the drop down menu to differentiate the head from the text.

Text heads organize the topics on a relational, hierarchical basis. For example, the paper title is the primary text head because all subsequent material relates and elaborates on this one topic. If there are two or more sub-topics, the next level head (uppercase Roman numerals) should be used and, conversely, if there are not at least two sub-topics, then no subheads should be introduced. Styles named “Heading 1”, “Heading 2”, “Heading 3”, and “Heading 4” are prescribed.
## Figures and Tables
####  Positioning Figures and Tables: Place figures and tables at the top and bottom of columns. Avoid placing them in the middle of columns. Large figures and tables may span across both columns. Figure captions should be below the figures; table heads should appear above the tables. Insert figures and tables after they are cited in the text. Use the abbreviation “Fig. 1”, even at the beginning of a sentence.

Figure Labels: Use 8 point Times New Roman for Figure labels. Use words rather than symbols or abbreviations when writing Figure axis labels to avoid confusing the reader. As an example, write the quantity “Magnetization”, or “Magnetization, M”, not just “M”. If including units in the label, present them within parentheses. Do not label axes only with units. In the example, write “Magnetization (A/m)” or “Magnetization {A[m(1)]}”, not just “A/m”. Do not label axes with a ratio of quantities and units. For example, write “Temperature (K)”, not “Temperature/K”.
##### Acknowledgment *(Heading 5)*
The preferred spelling of the word “acknowledgment” in America is without an “e” after the “g”. Avoid the stilted expression “one of us (R. B. G.) thanks ...”.  Instead, try “R. B. G. thanks...”. Put sponsor acknowledgments in the unnumbered footnote on the first page.
##### References
The template will number citations consecutively within brackets [1]. The sentence punctuation follows the bracket [2]. Refer simply to the reference number, as in [3]—do not use “Ref. [3]” or “reference [3]” except at the beginning of a sentence: “Reference [3] was the first ...”

Number footnotes separately in superscripts. Place the actual footnote at the bottom of the column in which it was cited. Do not put footnotes in the abstract or reference list. Use letters for table footnotes.

Unless there are six authors or more give all authors’ names; do not use “et al.”. Papers that have not been published, even if they have been submitted for publication, should be cited as “unpublished” [4]. Papers that have been accepted for publication should be cited as “in press” [5]. Capitalize only the first word in a paper title, except for proper nouns and element symbols.

For papers published in translation journals, please give the English citation first, followed by the original foreign-language citation [6].
